title: Théorie des cycles algébriques : conjectures de Hodge, Tate, Lefschetz, Weil : notes manuscrites (s.d.), lettre (1965).

deep.reconstruction:
This typed page is not Grothendieck's own mathematics. It is page 14 of a Bourbaki draft, 'Rédaction n° 391', and the sheet is photographed upside down. It was evidently reused as scrap paper in the Hodge/Tate/Lefschetz/Weil folder; the handwritten neighbouring pages, on theta divisors and Hodge-index sign computations, have nothing to do with it. The content belongs to the material that became Bourbaki, Lie Groups and Lie Algebras, Ch. V (groups generated by reflections), section on affine reflections.

Modern reading, step by step:

1. Let E be an affine space over a field K with translation space T (written ^vE).
2. Its homogenization (linearization) is ^hE = T × K, the vector space in which E sits as the affine hyperplane λ = 1.
3. An affine map u has linear part ^vu. Its homogenization ^hu is the linear map given by formula (9): (t, λ) ↦ (^vu(t) + λ(u(a) − a'), λ). The map u ↦ ^hu is injective.
4. An affine pseudo-reflection is an affine map s fixing pointwise an affine hyperplane H. Choosing an origin a in H makes s linear, so it is a pseudo-reflection in the linear sense of n° 2. Hence ^vs is a pseudo-reflection fixing the direction ^vH, and ^hs is a pseudo-reflection of ^hE fixing the hyperplane ^hH spanned by H.
5. An affine reflection is an involutive pseudo-reflection different from the identity. Equivalently, ^vs (or ^hs) is a reflection.
6. Now suppose char K ≠ 2 and Φ is a nondegenerate symmetric bilinear form on T. Then the reflections that are displacements (isometries) are exactly the orthogonal symmetries in non-isotropic affine hyperplanes (cross-references: Alg. IX §6 n° 6; n° 2, Prop. 4).
7. Proposition 9: let H and H' be parallel, non-isotropic hyperplanes. There is a unique t ⊥ H with H' = t + H, and the product s's of the two orthogonal symmetries is the translation by 2t.
8. Proof: take E = T with origin in H. Then s'(x) − t = s(x − t) = s(x) + t, because s(t) = −t. So s'(x) = s(x) + 2t and s's(x) = x + 2t.

The page serves the Bourbaki treatment of affine Weyl groups and groups generated by affine reflections, where products of parallel reflections give the translation lattice.
